nodes.label: Ṛgveda
nodes.sub: The Veda of praise: hymns to the powers of the cosmos. Its Upanishads ask what consciousness itself is.

nodes.label: Yajurveda
nodes.sub: The Veda of the sacrificial formulas (yajus), in two sections: the Śukla (‘white’), formulas kept apart from their explanation, and the Kṛṣṇa (‘black’), the two woven together. Its Upanishads turn the rite inward: the Self that is full, the chariot of the self, the five sheaths, the one God in all.

nodes.label: Sāmaveda
nodes.sub: The Veda of chant. Its Upanishads begin from the sung OM and end in ‘that thou art’.

nodes.label: Atharvaveda
nodes.sub: The Veda of everyday life and protection. Its Upanishads give the higher and lower knowledge, the six questions and the four states.

nodes.label: Wanting agreement, not evaluation
nodes.sub: The request asks to be backed up rather than to be looked at honestly.

nodes.label: Asking a source to say what you hope
nodes.sub: The request wants a quotation that fits a conclusion already reached.

nodes.label: Handing someone else the reins
nodes.sub: The request asks another to decide what only the person can decide.

nodes.label: Betting a life on a lucky streak
nodes.sub: A sudden gain is taken as proof, and a large, hard-to-undo decision follows.

nodes.label: Being told you are a genius
nodes.sub: The request asks for praise of an idea or a self, before testing it.

nodes.label: Pleasure that scrolls on
nodes.sub: Attention pulled outward by what is designed to hold it.

nodes.label: Wanting to hurt the one who hurt you
nodes.sub: The request asks for help to wound, expose or humiliate.

nodes.label: Grief and the fear of ending
nodes.sub: The question of what remains when someone dies, or when one will.

nodes.label: Knowing a lot, understanding little
nodes.sub: Learning accumulates, but the sorrow it was meant to address does not lift.

nodes.label: Exhaustion and the right to rest
nodes.sub: Pushing on past depletion, and doubting whether rest is allowed.

nodes.label: Living someone else's choice to keep the peace
nodes.sub: The request asks for permission to give up one's own path because family expects another, and to be told that doing so is right.

nodes.label: Measuring one's worth against others
nodes.sub: The request asks for relief from comparison by a verdict: either 'you are behind' or 'it does not matter at all'.

nodes.label: Śaunaka
nodes.sub: householder who asks the one question

nodes.label: Aśvapati Kaikeya
nodes.sub: king who teaches the Vaiśvānara self

nodes.label: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali
nodes.sub: king who teaches the five fires

nodes.label: Śāṇḍilya
nodes.sub: sage of the meditation on Brahman

nodes.label: Naciketas and Death
nodes.sub: A boy given away to Death waits three nights at his door, is offered every pleasure in exchange for his question, and refuses them all.

nodes.label: Indra and Virocana
nodes.sub: Two students hear Prajāpati's first answer. Virocana leaves satisfied and teaches it to his people; Indra sees the flaw, returns three times, and is taught the truth after a hundred and one years.

nodes.label: Satyakāma tells the truth
nodes.sub: Asked his lineage, a boy repeats his mother's honest answer that she does not know it. The teacher accepts him because he did not swerve from the truth.

nodes.label: Uddālaka teaches Śvetaketu: “that thou art”
nodes.sub: Śvetaketu returns from twelve years of study, proud and unable to say what makes the unheard heard. His father teaches him with clay, honey, rivers, a tree, a banyan seed and salt dissolved in water, and nine times says: that thou art.

nodes.label: Nārada knows the texts
nodes.sub: Nārada lists every science he has mastered and admits he is still in sorrow: he knows the words, not the Self. Sanatkumāra leads him to the boundless.

nodes.label: Maitreyī's question
nodes.sub: Offered half of a household's wealth, Maitreyī asks the only question that matters: 'What should I do with that which will not make me immortal?'

nodes.label: Bhṛgu learns by inquiry
nodes.sub: Bhṛgu asks his father for Brahman. Varuṇa gives him clues and sends him to find out. Five times Bhṛgu returns with a deeper answer, until he reaches bliss.

nodes.label: The gods and the Yakṣa
nodes.sub: The gods take a victory for their own. A mysterious being sets a blade of grass before Agni and Vāyu, who cannot burn or move it. Umā tells Indra who it was.

nodes.label: Sukeśa will not lie
nodes.sub: Sukeśa tells his teacher Pippalāda how a prince once asked him about the person of sixteen parts, and how he answered plainly that he did not know, because one who speaks untruth withers to the root.

nodes.label: Gārgī questions Yājñavalkya
nodes.sub: At Janaka's great debate, Gārgī presses Yājñavalkya on what the worlds are woven upon until he warns her not to ask too far; she returns with two questions like arrows and is answered with the Imperishable.

nodes.label: Janaka and the light of the person
nodes.sub: King Janaka asks Yājñavalkya what light a person has: the sun, the moon, fire, speech; and when all are gone, the Self is the light.

nodes.label: Six seekers before Pippalāda
nodes.sub: Six students come to the sage Pippalāda with fuel in hand. He makes them live a year in austerity, then answers six questions: on creation, breath, its rising and setting, sleep, OM and the Person of sixteen parts.

nodes.label: Śaunaka asks Aṅgiras
nodes.sub: The great householder Śaunaka asks: what is that by knowing which all this is known? Aṅgiras answers with the two knowledges, the lower and the higher.

nodes.label: Jānaśruti and Raikva the cart-man
nodes.sub: A generous king overhears two swans praising a sage who sits under a cart scratching his itch. He offers cattle and gold; Raikva sends him away until he comes with real humility.

nodes.label: Upakosala and the fires
nodes.sub: A student tends his teacher's fires for twelve years and falls ill with longing; the fires themselves teach him that Brahman is breath, joy and space.

nodes.label: Aśvapati and the universal self
nodes.sub: Five learned householders and Uddālaka go to King Aśvapati, each worshipping a part of the self; he teaches them the self that is all of it.

nodes.label: Pravāhaṇa and the five fires
nodes.sub: Śvetaketu, proud of his learning, cannot answer King Pravāhaṇa's five questions about where beings go after death. His father comes humbly to learn the teaching of the five fires.

nodes.label: Ajātaśatru and the proud Bālāki
nodes.sub: Bālāki offers to teach the king Brahman and names twelve forms of it; each is refuted, and the king leads him to a sleeping man to show where the self goes in sleep.

nodes.label: Citra questions Śvetaketu
nodes.sub: King Citra asks the young priest where the worlds after death end; neither son nor father knows, and both come to learn from the king.

nodes.label: Indra teaches Pratardana
nodes.sub: The king Pratardana wins his way to Indra's world and asks for the boon most beneficial to humans; Indra teaches him that he is prāṇa, the conscious self.

nodes.label: King Bṛhadratha in the forest
nodes.sub: Weary of a body made of bones, skin and decay, King Bṛhadratha gives up his kingdom and stands a thousand years in austerity until the sage Śākāyanya teaches him the Self.

nodes.label: The Self creates the worlds
nodes.sub: In the beginning the Self alone was; it thought, let me create the worlds, then their guardians, then food; and finally it entered the person through the crown of the head.

nodes.label: Uṣasti eats the elephant-keeper's beans
nodes.sub: In a famine a starving priest eats an elephant-keeper's leftover beans but refuses his water: one bends a rule to live, not for comfort. He then questions the court priests on the gods they chant to.

nodes.label: The thunder says Da, Da, Da
nodes.sub: Gods, humans and demons ask Prajāpati for teaching; to each he says only 'Da'. The gods hear restrain, the humans give, the demons be compassionate, and the thunder repeats it still.

nodes.label: Śāṇḍilya's meditation
nodes.sub: All this is Brahman. The self within the heart is smaller than a grain of rice and greater than the earth: Śāṇḍilya's teaching on how to meditate on it.

nodes.label: Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court
nodes.sub: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the most learned of the Brahmins. Yājñavalkya has them driven away before anyone answers; one by one the court's scholars question him, from Aśvala to Gārgī and Śākalya, and none prevails.

nodes.label: The gods, the demons and the breath
nodes.sub: The gods chant the Udgītha to overcome the demons; each sense chants and is pierced by evil, until the breath in the mouth chants and the demons shatter against it like clods against a rock.

nodes.label: The dogs' Udgītha
nodes.sub: A satire on ritual for gain: hungry dogs ask a white dog to chant the Udgītha for food, and parade like priests before the hymn: ‘Om, let us eat! Om, let us drink!’

nodes.label: Three sages on the Udgītha
nodes.sub: Three learned men ask one another what the chant rests on; each answer is taken one step further, from heaven to space, until King Pravāhaṇa names space as the final support.
